title: Pave motion audit
subtitle: Every place in the front end where something moves, read and scored against one motion language.
author: Alexander Traykov
summary: About 750 transitions and animations across about 350 stylesheets became 47 proposed fixes.
The same spinner ran at four different speeds, because its keyframes were copied from file to file.
The browser default `ease` speeds up before it slows down, so entrances feel late.
The marketing hero moved all the time; the product grid moves about a quarter of the time.

sections.title: How it was read
sections.takeaway: Every stylesheet was read, not sampled.
text: Each place where something moves was scored on four things: duration, easing, the property animated and what happens under reduced motion. Findings that broke the motion language became proposed fixes.

sections.title: One spinner, four speeds
sections.takeaway: A slow spinner makes the app feel slow at the same load time.
text: The keyframes had been copied from file to file, and each copy drifted. The fix was one shared keyframe at 0.8 seconds.

sections.note: Whatever a spinner is made of, define its speed once.

sections.title: What a finding looks like
sections.takeaway: Each finding shows how long the motion takes and how its speed changes, today against proposed.
text: The duration ruler is 20 cells of 25 ms on a fixed 500 ms scale, so every finding in the report compares with every other one. The speed glyph shows how much progress happens in each eighth of the time.

sections.title: What it cost to get right
sections.takeaway: The glyph code had two bugs that reached the published audit.
text: 25 of the 47 findings showed the wrong easing name next to a correct glyph: the parser took the first CSS variable it found, which was a speed multiplier. And a value of 57 out of 100 drew one cell short, because a rounding remainder of 8/8 had no glyph. Both are covered by tests now.
